title: The Broken Promise and the Marshmallow
text:
Celeste Kidd, Holly Palmeri and Richard Aslin at the University of Rochester added a twist to the classic marshmallow test. Kidd had once volunteered at a homeless shelter, where she noticed that children grabbed food immediately, for the sensible reason that anything left unclaimed could vanish.

The researchers gave children aged three to five an art project. Each child received a worn set of crayons and was told that if they waited, the researcher would bring a bigger, better set. For half the children, the researcher came back with the promised crayons. For the other half, she returned empty-handed and apologized. The same thing happened with a promise of nice stickers.

Then came the standard test: a marshmallow on the table, and the promise of a second one if the child waited. The difference was large. Children who had just experienced a reliable adult waited, on average, about four times longer than children whose adult had broken her promises. Many in the reliable group lasted the full fifteen minutes; few in the unreliable group did.

The study suggested that a child who eats the marshmallow quickly may not lack self-control at all. They may simply be making a reasonable judgment about whether the adults around them keep their word.
lesson: Children will only wait for a reward they believe in. If you want patience from others, start by keeping your promises.
people: Celeste Kidd, Holly Palmeri, Richard Aslin
source: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., and Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114.
caveat: The study was small, with 28 children, though later work has supported the role of trust in children's waiting.
